title: The Avenue Victor Hugo to Recoleta: Sugar Nucleotides, and a Nobel Prize Won in a Borrowed Building
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Address on the Avenue Victor Hugo

stops.name: Paris, 81 Avenue Victor Hugo: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; both encyclopedic sources give the day, the month and the street number
stops.campa: At number 81 of the Avenue Victor Hugo, in the sixteenth arrondissement, an Argentine couple travelling in France has a son on the sixth of September 1906. They are landowners of Basque descent whose estancia lies on the Atlantic coast of Buenos Aires province; no source consulted names the Basque town the family came from. The child is French by the accident of an address. Forty-one years later Eva Peron will be received in this same city on the Rainbow Tour, at a different quarter and for different reasons; the overlap is geography and nothing else.
suggested_refs: The building at 81 Avenue Victor Hugo, 75116 Paris, cited by biographers as the exact birthplace

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, the return crossing
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day unknown and defaulted to January the first
stops.campa: In 1908 the family recrosses the Atlantic and the boy comes ashore at the port his parents call home, at the docks where the immigrant ships of the great Argentine influx are tying up week after week. No biographer names the pier or the ship; the crossing is certain and its particulars are not. He enters, at two years old, a country he has never seen. He will leave it afterwards to study, to work in other men's laboratories and to collect prizes, and each time he comes back to this city and to no other.
suggested_refs: Passenger and immigration records of the Port of Buenos Aires, 1908, not located in this research
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Luis Federico Leloir' (port and ship unspecified)

stops.name: Estancia El Tuyu, the pampa childhood
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; sources place the boyhood on the estancia without pinning years
stops.campa: The boyhood runs on El Tuyu, the family estancia stretched along the coast between San Clemente del Tuyu and Mar de Ajo, a holding biographers count in tens of thousands of hectares. Cattle, dune grass and a flat horizon are the first landscape he learns. No source consulted explains how a son of this class arrived at enzymes; the biographies record the estancia and they record the laboratory, and they leave the road between them blank. The rest of his working life will be spent indoors, at a bench, over sugars, within a few kilometres of one capital.
suggested_refs: Cadastral records of the Estancia El Tuyu between San Clemente del Tuyu and Mar de Ajo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Escuela General San Martin and Colegio Lacordaire
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source gives enrolment years for either school
stops.campa: Schooling begins at the Escuela General San Martin in Buenos Aires and continues at Colegio Lacordaire, run in the Dominican tradition. Neither building is fixed by street address in any source consulted here, so the pin stands for the school's historical quarter of the city rather than a verified door. What the sources do fix is the pattern: confessional schools, for a family that will also send him to England and to Paris, an education arranged at home and abroad at once. No years are given for either enrolment, and no subject he studied in them is named.
suggested_refs: Enrolment registers of the Escuela General San Martin and Colegio Lacordaire, Buenos Aires, not located

stops.name: Colegio del Salvador, Avenida Callao: the Jesuit years
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; attendance attested, years not given by the source
stops.campa: At Colegio del Salvador, the Jesuit school on Avenida Callao, he finishes his secondary education among the sons of the capital's established families. The institution was founded in the nineteenth century and teaches still. It gives him the classical grounding expected before university, and the plan is medicine, not chemistry. The Facultad de Medicina waits a few blocks away on Avenida Cordoba; the Manzana de las Luces, where he will meet his first chemistry, waits in the old city centre. His record does not yet name a laboratory.
suggested_refs: Colegio del Salvador, Avenida Callao 542, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Beaumont College, Old Windsor: the English interval
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the stay is attested, the dates are fixed by no source consulted
stops.campa: For a period whose dates no source fixes, he is sent to Beaumont College at Old Windsor, the Jesuit boarding school on the Thames near Runnymede that educated Catholic gentry from Britain and abroad between 1861 and 1967. It is his first extended stay in England, and it is short. He will come back to the country as a young scientist, to Cambridge and to Frederick Gowland Hopkins. That second English residence is often described as running seven years; the prose of the same source says he was home in Buenos Aires after about one.
suggested_refs: Beaumont College, Old Windsor, Berkshire, operating 1861 to 1967

stops.name: Paris, rue Descartes: architecture abandoned
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; neither the year nor the institution is settled by the sources
stops.campa: He enrols in Paris to study architecture and abandons it. English sources call the school the Ecole Polytechnique, Spanish sources the Institut Polytechnique, and neither institution taught architecture; the claim as written is attested by no source and contradicted between two. The rue Descartes campus the Ecole occupied until 1976 stands in for an address nobody has fixed. What survives the contradiction is the shape of the episode: a false start in the city of his birth, and a return to Buenos Aires to read medicine instead.
suggested_refs: The former Ecole Polytechnique campus, rue Descartes, Paris, occupied until 1976
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Luis Federico Leloir' (name conflict unresolved)

segments.name: Medicine, and the Turn to the Bench

stops.name: Mar del Plata, the invention of salsa golf
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the mid-1920s dating rests on repetition, not on a document
stops.campa: Tradition holds that at the golf club at Mar del Plata, tired of plain mayonnaise on his shrimp, the young man mixes mayonnaise with ketchup and invents what Argentina will eat ever after as salsa golf. Spanish Wikipedia calls the account one of many versions of tradition; English Wikipedia sets the scene at the Ocean Club instead, a different place on the same coast. No primary source or contemporary account has been located. The country keeps the story because it likes it, and because he never patented the sauce.
stops.quote: Si hubiera patentado esa salsa, tendriamos mucho mas dinero para investigar en este momento.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Leloir in Infobae, 5 September 2017, 'Salsa golf: la historia del invento gastronomico de un Premio Nobel argentino', which introduces the line as 'Dijo algo asi como', that is, approximate wording the outlet does not vouch for
suggested_refs: The Mar del Plata Golf Club, Lomas de Stella Maris; and the rival Ocean Club attribution in English-language sources

stops.name: Facultad de Medicina, Avenida Cordoba: the medical degree
stops.date_confidence: year attested by both sources; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: In 1932 he takes his medical degree from the Facultad de Medicina of the Universidad de Buenos Aires on Avenida Cordoba, the course his Paris detour delayed. English Wikipedia reports, without a document behind it, that anatomy cost him four attempts. The degree qualifies him to practise, and he practises for a few years only. Within a decade he has left the ward for the bench; within two he directs an institute of his own. None of that is visible in 1932, when he is a newly graduated Argentine physician among several hundred others.
suggested_refs: Diploma records of the Facultad de Medicina, Universidad de Buenos Aires, 1932

stops.name: Hospital de Clinicas Jose de San Martin, the residency
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the residency is attested, its dates are not itemized
stops.campa: He serves his residency at the Hospital de Clinicas Jose de San Martin, the teaching hospital of the university medical school. Ward rounds and patients occupy these years, and they are the years in which the medicine of the 1930s shows him its limits. The building he trained in no longer stands: the nineteenth-century Hospital de Clinicas on Avenida Cordoba was demolished and its ground is now Plaza Houssay, named for the man who is about to take him on. The institution still trains Argentine doctors; the walls do not.
stops.quote: we could do little for our patients... antibiotics, psychoactive drugs, and all the new therapeutic agents were unknown
stops.quote_source: Luis F. Leloir, 'Far Away and Long Ago', Annual Review of Biochemistry 52 (1983), as excerpted in the Wikipedia article; the full original is behind the Annual Reviews paywall and was not retrieved
suggested_refs: Plaza Houssay, Buenos Aires, on the site of the demolished nineteenth-century Hospital de Clinicas
sources: Luis F. Leloir, 'Far Away and Long Ago' (1983), via secondary excerpt

stops.name: Hospital Ramos Mejia, Balvanera: the second internship
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; internship attested without dates, placed in the early 1930s
stops.campa: He interns as well at the Hospital General de Agudos Jose Maria Ramos Mejia on General Urquiza in Balvanera, a hospital treating the acute cases of a working capital. His biographers record the posting and do not dwell on it. It is a required stage on the way to somewhere else. In these same years he begins taking the chemistry courses he was never given as a medical student. The sources attest the courses. None of them records the month or the argument in which he decided that the bedside was not where he would stay.
suggested_refs: Hospital General de Agudos Jose Maria Ramos Mejia, General Urquiza 609, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Facultad de Medicina, the Instituto de Fisiologia: Houssay takes him on
stops.date_confidence: year given by Spanish Wikipedia; month reconstructed
stops.campa: Bernardo Houssay, who runs the Instituto de Fisiologia inside the Facultad de Medicina building on Paraguay, takes him as a doctoral student and sets him on the adrenal glands and carbohydrate metabolism. Spanish Wikipedia reports the introduction came through the family, by way of his cousin Victoria Ocampo, and offers no document for it. Houssay will go to Stockholm in 1947 as the first Argentine science laureate, and Leloir will follow him there in 1970. In this year they are in this building together, one of them a professor with a chair and the other a physician who has decided to start again.
suggested_refs: The Instituto de Fisiologia of Bernardo Houssay, housed in the Facultad de Medicina at Paraguay 2155

stops.name: Manzana de las Luces, Peru 222: the first chemistry
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; attendance attested, years not fixed by the source
stops.campa: Not satisfied with a medical degree, he takes courses at the Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales, then housed in the Manzana de las Luces on Peru in the old city centre, a colonial block that has held Jesuit, viceregal and university institutions in turn. It is his first formal chemistry, taken as a graduate physician sitting among undergraduates. The distance between this room and the Stockholm Concert Hall is thirty-six years and one question, repeated: what carries a sugar from one molecule to another.
suggested_refs: The Manzana de las Luces, Peru 222, Buenos Aires, then housing the Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the doctoral thesis on the adrenal glands
stops.date_confidence: year corrected to 1934; both sources say the thesis took two years from the 1932 diploma, and the 1935 date circulating in secondary accounts fits neither
stops.campa: The thesis on the adrenal glands and carbohydrate metabolism, written under Houssay, is judged the best doctoral work of the medical faculty that year and takes the faculty prize. Two years of work stand behind it, counted from the 1932 diploma. The subject is already the subject: how the body handles sugar. Thirty-six years later, standing in Stockholm, he will name a single person as the influence on his whole research career, and it will be the man who directed this thesis, in this faculty, in these two years.
stops.quote: My whole research career has been influenced by one person, Prof. Bernardo A. Houssay, who directed my doctoral thesis and who during all these years generously gave me his invaluable advice and friendship.
stops.quote_source: Luis F. Leloir, 'Two Decades of Research on the Biosynthesis of Saccharides', Nobel Lecture, Stockholm, 12 December 1970
suggested_refs: The 1934 doctoral thesis of Luis F. Leloir, Facultad de Medicina, Universidad de Buenos Aires

segments.name: Cambridge, and the Year the University Closed

stops.name: Cambridge, Tennis Court Road: the year with Hopkins
stops.date_confidence: year of arrival attested; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: He works in the Sir William Dunn Institute of Biochemistry on Tennis Court Road under Frederick Gowland Hopkins, the discoverer of vitamins and himself a Nobel laureate, on enzymatic effects including those of cyanide and pyrophosphate. Cambridge gives him the enzymology that Buenos Aires medicine could not. The stay is often printed as running to 1943, which is an infobox range; the prose of the same source says he was back in Buenos Aires in 1937 after a brief stay. This journey follows the prose.
suggested_refs: The Sir William Dunn Institute of Biochemistry, Tennis Court Road, Cambridge, under F. G. Hopkins

stops.name: Buenos Aires, back at Houssay's institute
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the prose of English Wikipedia; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: He returns to Buenos Aires in 1937 and resumes work under Houssay, and for six years the two men do carbohydrate and adrenal physiology in the same institute. This is the stretch that later accounts dissolve into a phantom Cambridge decade running 1936 to 1943. It is six settled years in a state university, and the state university is where the next decade of Argentine politics will be fought out. He is thirty-one when the six years begin and thirty-seven when they end, and the ending is not his decision.
suggested_refs: Publications of Leloir and Houssay, Instituto de Fisiologia, Buenos Aires, 1937 to 1943

stops.name: Buenos Aires, marriage to Amelia Zuberbuhler
stops.date_confidence: year attested; no source names the month, the church or the civil registry
stops.campa: He marries Amelia Zuberbuhler in Buenos Aires in the year everything else moves. The venue is named by no biographer, so the pin stands for the city. English Wikipedia records one daughter, also called Amelia; Spanish Wikipedia says four children. The discrepancy is not resolved here and should not be quietly split. What is certain is the timing: a household established in the same twelve months in which he loses his university post and leaves the country for two years of foreign laboratories.
suggested_refs: Civil marriage records, Buenos Aires, 1943, not located in this research
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Luis Federico Leloir' (child count in conflict)

stops.name: Casa Rosada, the coup of 4 June 1943
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the fourth of June the GOU takes the Casa Rosada, the coup that opens the road for Juan Peron. Within months the new government begins purging the universities of professors who signed the anti-Nazi declaration, and Houssay loses his chair. Three years later the same climate will push Jorge Luis Borges out of the Miguel Cane library. Leloir is not in the building. The building decides where the rest of his working life will be spent.
suggested_refs: The Casa Rosada, Plaza de Mayo, seat of the 4 June 1943 GOU coup

stops.name: Universidad de Buenos Aires, the resignation
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Spanish Wikipedia; month reconstructed as following the mid-year purge
stops.campa: Houssay is stripped of his university chair under the Ramirez military government for signing a declaration against the Axis. Leloir resigns his own post in solidarity, and leaves the state system that trained him. Spanish Wikipedia frames the resignation as an act of loyalty; English Wikipedia's infobox blurs the year into a Cambridge range and obscures it. He is thirty-seven, without a laboratory and without a salary, and he leaves for the United States before the year ends.
suggested_refs: The 1943 university purges under the Pedro Pablo Ramirez government

stops.name: St. Louis, the Cori laboratory
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed
stops.campa: He crosses to Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis and works in the pharmacology department, in the laboratory of Carl and Gerty Cori, whose own Nobel Prize for glycogen metabolism is four years ahead of them. Secondary accounts give him the rank of associate professor; neither cited source supports a faculty title, and he is better described as a visiting researcher. The Coris are working out how the body breaks glycogen down and builds it back up. He arrives in that room a physician who has done adrenal physiology, and he leaves it working on sugar.
suggested_refs: The Cori laboratory, Department of Pharmacology, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis

stops.name: Columbia, College of Physicians and Surgeons: enzyme research
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: In 1944 he moves to the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Columbia University on West 168th Street as a research assistant in an enzyme laboratory, while the war in Europe is still running. It is the last American posting and the shortest. Twenty-three years later this same university will give him the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize, and he will return to a campus where he once did bench work as a foreigner on a temporary contract, to be handed a medal for what he did afterwards somewhere else.
suggested_refs: Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons, 630 West 168th Street, New York

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the return for good
stops.date_confidence: year attested by both sources; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: He comes home in 1945 to work again with Houssay, and the itinerary closes: Buenos Aires, Cambridge, St. Louis, New York, Buenos Aires. From here his geography collapses to a handful of addresses in one city, and it stays collapsed for forty-two years. The offers to leave will keep arriving, from the Rockefeller Foundation and from Massachusetts General Hospital among others, and he will keep declining them. Everything he is remembered for is done within a few kilometres of this building.
suggested_refs: Leloir and Houssay's joint work, Buenos Aires, 1945 to 1947

stops.name: Julian Alvarez, Palermo: the Instituto Campomar founded
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: At Houssay's initiative the textile industrialist Jaime Campomar funds a private biochemical institute at a hundred thousand pesos a month, and Leloir directs it from a house on Julian Alvarez in Palermo. English Wikipedia gives the number as 1719, the Spanish article on the institute gives 1917; the conflict is unresolved here. In the same years Peron's government pushes Jorge Luis Borges out of his municipal library post. The laboratory that will produce Argentina's Nobel Prize in Chemistry opens outside the state system, four years after Leloir resigned from it.
stops.quote: No existen problemas agotados, solo hay hombres agotados por los problemas.
stops.quote_source: The phrase Leloir posted at the entrance of the Instituto de Investigaciones Bioquimicas de la Fundacion Campomar, per Federico Pergola, 'Historia de la Medicina argentina' (Eudeba), quoted in La Prensa, 'Houssay, Leloir y Milstein: vivir para la ciencia' (live URL now 404, retrieved via the Wayback Machine); not documented as a saying he coined
suggested_refs: The first house of the Fundacion Campomar on Julian Alvarez, Palermo, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Palermo, the sugar nucleotides identified
stops.date_confidence: the pathway work runs from 1948; the isolation of UDP-glucose is placed in 1949 to 1950, and the exact month is not fixed
stops.campa: With improvised equipment in a converted house, his team isolates uridine diphosphate glucose and shows that sugar nucleotides are the intermediates by which carbohydrates are built. It is the discovery. Twenty-two years later the Royal Swedish Academy will describe it in a single line of prize motivation. The Sociedad Cientifica Argentina gives him a prize for the work in these years, though the source does not name the year. No source consulted records how many people were at the bench with him.
stops.quote: Our work on the biosynthesis of oligo- and polysaccharides started about in 1946 not by a deliberate selection of the subject but because it came to us.
stops.quote_source: Luis F. Leloir, 'Two Decades of Research on the Biosynthesis of Saccharides', Nobel Lecture, Stockholm, 12 December 1970
suggested_refs: The 1949 to 1950 papers on uridine diphosphate glucose from the Instituto Campomar

stops.name: Palermo, galactose and the Leloir pathway
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the work runs through the 1950s and no source pins a year
stops.campa: Through the 1950s the institute maps galactose metabolism, the route that will carry his name, and works out the biochemical basis of galactosemia, the inherited disorder in which a child cannot process the sugar in milk. He is also named titular professor at the biochemical institute of the university in 1949, a post reported by one source only. The pathway carries his name in the textbooks that teach it. It was worked out in a converted house in Palermo, by a team paid out of a textile fortune, in a country with no research funding to speak of.
suggested_refs: The Leloir pathway of galactose metabolism, as set out in the institute's papers of the 1950s

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the funding crisis and the refusals
stops.date_confidence: year given by Spanish Wikipedia only; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Jaime Campomar dies and the institute that carries his money nearly closes. Leloir is offered places at the Rockefeller Foundation and at Massachusetts General Hospital in the United States and turns both down, then secures grants from the National Institutes of Health and from Rockefeller to keep the laboratory in Argentina. Spanish Wikipedia carries the episode; no primary document was reached for it. The refusals are the reason the Leloir pathway has an Argentine address and not an American one.
suggested_refs: NIH and Rockefeller Foundation grant records for the Instituto Campomar, from 1957

stops.name: Vuelta de Obligado and Monroe, the girls' school
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: The Argentine government donates a building formerly used as a girls' school, at the corner of Vuelta de Obligado and Monroe, under an agreement signed with Dean Rolando Garcia of the Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales. The institute moves out of Palermo. The intersection is named in the sources but no survey of the building was reached, so the pin here is the canonical Belgrano coordinate already used for Bernardo Houssay's IBYME, a few blocks along the same street. Everything of the second half of his career, the Nobel Prize included, comes out of this donated schoolhouse.
suggested_refs: The former girls' school at Vuelta de Obligado and Monroe, Belgrano, home of the institute from 1958

stops.name: Columbia University, the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Columbia University awards him the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize, a biology and biochemistry honour that many of its holders have taken a few years before a Nobel Prize. He had worked at Columbia's College of Physicians and Surgeons in 1944 and 1945, as a research assistant on a temporary contract. The university that gave him a bench gives him a medal twenty-three years later. It is the first honour of the run that ends in Stockholm, and it comes from outside Argentina.
suggested_refs: The Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize of Columbia University, 1967

stops.name: Casina Pio IV, Vatican City: the Pontifical Academy
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: He is elected to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, which meets in the Casina Pio IV inside the Vatican gardens, a body whose lineage runs back to the academies of Galileo's century and whose mandate is scientific rather than doctrinal. He was schooled by Dominicans at Lacordaire and by Jesuits at Colegio del Salvador and at Beaumont, and the Academy elects him for the biochemistry rather than for the schooling. Two further honours reach him in the same year, and the Nobel Prize two years after that.
suggested_refs: The Casina Pio IV, seat of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, Vatican City

stops.name: Universidad Nacional de Cordoba, the honorary doctorate
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Argentina's oldest university, founded by Jesuits in 1613, gives him an honorary doctorate. Cordoba predates by nearly three centuries the Buenos Aires institutions where he actually trained, and it is honouring a career built entirely in the capital. The doctorate falls in the same year as Mexico's Premio Benito Juarez and the Vatican election. The Argentine honours arrive nineteen years after the sugar nucleotides were isolated and two years before the Nobel Prize, which is the order in which such things usually arrive.
suggested_refs: The honorary doctorate of the Universidad Nacional de Cordoba, 1968

stops.name: Mexico City, the Premio Benito Juarez
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Mexico awards him the Premio Benito Juarez, named for the nineteenth-century president and reformer. No source consulted names the ceremony's venue, so the capital stands in as the likeliest host and is flagged as reconstruction rather than record. It is the Latin American honour in the 1968 cluster, given by one country of the region to a laboratory in another, and it precedes by two years the Stockholm decision that the rest of the world will cite instead.
suggested_refs: The Premio Benito Juarez, Mexico, 1968, ceremony venue unlocated

stops.name: Stockholm Concert Hall, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the tenth of December, Gustaf VI Adolf hands him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, sole laureate, the first Ibero-American to take that prize. He is the second Argentine science laureate after Houssay, who stood on this same stage in 1947 and whose Buenos Aires chair, lost to a coup twenty-seven years earlier, is the reason Leloir built his career in a donated schoolhouse instead of a national laboratory. The same platform, the same month and day, twice over for two men who once worked the same corridor.
stops.quote: for his discovery of sugar nucleotides and their role in the biosynthesis of carbohydrates
stops.quote_source: Official prize motivation of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1970; the Academy's words about Leloir, not his own
suggested_refs: The Stockholm Concert Hall at Hotorget, site of the Nobel award ceremonies

stops.name: Stockholm City Hall, the banquet in the Blue Hall
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The banquet follows in the Blue Hall of the City Hall, a room Ragnar Ostberg designed for exactly this kind of evening decades before any of the year's laureates were chosen. Leloir speaks briefly, names van 't Hoff and Fischer and Arrhenius and Ramsay and von Baeyer as the company his name is now joining, says he is uneasy about it, and credits the collaborators who did a great part of the work. He is a man who drives a Fiat 600 to a converted school in Belgrano.
stops.quote: Finally, I might paraphrase Churchill and say: never have I received so much for so little.
stops.quote_source: Luis F. Leloir, Nobel Banquet speech, Stockholm City Hall, 10 December 1970; a deliberate echo of Churchill's 1940 Battle of Britain address
suggested_refs: The Blue Hall of Stockholm City Hall, site of the Nobel banquet

stops.name: Stockholm, the Nobel lecture on two decades of saccharides
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the lecture hall is not named in the sources reached, and the pin stands for the city
stops.campa: Two days after the ceremony he delivers the lecture, titled Two Decades of Research on the Biosynthesis of Saccharides. He tells the hall the work began in 1946 not because he selected the subject but because it came to him, calls his own first experiments Paleolithic by the standards of what biochemistry has since become, and thanks Houssay by name. The nobelprize.org pages for his biography and facts returned 403 to this research; the lecture text itself was reached as a Nobel Foundation PDF.
stops.quote: Due to the phenomenal progress of biochemistry our initial experiments seem to belong to the Paleolithic period but fortunately there are also some very recent and exciting advances in the field.
stops.quote_source: Luis F. Leloir, 'Two Decades of Research on the Biosynthesis of Saccharides', Nobel Lecture, Stockholm, 12 December 1970 (Nobel Foundation PDF)
suggested_refs: 'Two Decades of Research on the Biosynthesis of Saccharides', Nobel Lecture PDF, Nobel Foundation

stops.name: Belgrano, champagne in test tubes and the prize money given away
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the celebration and the donation are attested for 1970, the day is not
stops.campa: Back at the institute the team drinks champagne out of laboratory test tubes, and the whole prize sum, about eighty thousand dollars, goes into research. He keeps none of it. Asked to explain the discovery to a magazine, he refuses the word feat and corrects the pronoun in mid-sentence, from I to my team. The Fiat 600 that carries him to work each morning is cited by every Argentine journalist who writes about him afterwards, precisely because it contradicts what Nobel science is supposed to look like.
stops.quote: Lo que hice es dificil de entender. Es solo un paso de una larga investigacion. Descubri (no yo: mi equipo) la funcion de los nucleotidos azucares en el metabolismo celular. Yo quisiera que lo entendieran, pero no es facil explicarlo. Tampoco es una hazana: es apenas saber un poco mas...
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Leloir on receiving news of the prize, Revista Gente, reproduced on the Comodoro Rivadavia articles page at elchenque.com.ar (site defunct, retrieved via the Wayback Machine capture of 28 February 2007); the English versions in circulation are loose translations
suggested_refs: Revista Gente's 1970 interview with Leloir, surviving only in a defunct site's archived copy

stops.name: The Royal Society, Carlton House Terrace: Foreign Member
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: The Royal Society elects him a Foreign Member at its house on Carlton House Terrace. He had come to England twice, once as a schoolboy at Beaumont and once for a single year at Cambridge, and had built nothing there. London joins Stockholm, Mexico City, Cordoba and the Vatican on the list of places formally recognising work done entirely in Buenos Aires. The recognition travels; he travels only to collect it and to come home again to the converted school in Belgrano, which he is still directing at sixty-six.
suggested_refs: Royal Society election records, Foreign Members, 1972

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Legion of Honour from France
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown, and the source does not say whether the ceremony was in Paris or at the embassy in Buenos Aires
stops.campa: France makes him a member of the Legion of Honour, seventy-six years after he was born on the Avenue Victor Hugo and never lived in the country again. No source names the ceremony's location, so the French embassy on Cerrito stands in as the likelier of the two candidates for a man of that age settled in Buenos Aires; the alternative is Paris itself. Venezuela had given him the Orden de Andres Bello in 1971 and Chile the Gran Cruz of the Orden de Bernardo O'Higgins in 1976.
suggested_refs: The French embassy in Buenos Aires, Cerrito 1399, as probable but unconfirmed site of the 1982 investiture

stops.name: Trieste, the Third World Academy of Sciences
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: He is among the founders of the Third World Academy of Sciences at Trieste, an institution built on the proposition that research done in poor countries is research and not charity. He is the case in point: a Nobel Prize in Chemistry taken out of a donated schoolhouse funded by a textile manufacturer, with grants raised abroad and equipment improvised at home. No source consulted says whether he was at Trieste in person. The Argentine Konex jury gives him the Premio Konex de Brillante in the same year.
suggested_refs: Founding documents of the Third World Academy of Sciences, Trieste, 1983

stops.name: Parque Centenario, the institute's third home
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the Spanish article on the institute; month reconstructed
stops.campa: The institute moves a third time, into a purpose-built facility on Avenida Patricias Argentinas by Parque Centenario, later expanded from six thousand nine hundred to ten thousand nine hundred square metres. He is seventy-seven and still directing it. Julian Alvarez held the institute from 1947 to 1958 and Vuelta de Obligado from 1958 to 1983, so the four decades of daily commuting to a single Palermo address that some accounts describe cannot have happened; the forty years went to three different doors. No source consulted names the architect of the new building.
suggested_refs: The Instituto Leloir building, Avenida Patricias Argentinas 435, by Parque Centenario

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Ciudadano Ilustre
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the chamber in which the honour was conferred is not confirmed, and the pin is set to the Legislatura's historic seat on Peru
stops.campa: The City of Buenos Aires names him Ciudadano Ilustre, the honorific it reserves for residents whose work brings distinction to the capital. No source consulted fixes the hall, so the Legislatura's seat on Peru stands in, flagged as reconstruction. It is the local counterpart to the honours that have been arriving from abroad since Stockholm: the city formally claiming, in 1984, a man it has informally claimed since a two-year-old came off a ship at its docks in 1908.
suggested_refs: Legislatura de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, Peru 130, probable site of the 1984 conferral

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the lecture on scientific research in Argentina
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date is given in the published citation of the conference text
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of June he delivers an address titled Comentarios sobre la investigacion cientifica en la Argentina, published the following year by the institute for the theory, organisation and history of science. He is seventy-eight, two and a half years from his death, speaking to a country whose research funding has never once been secure in his lifetime. Cesar Milstein, who trained in this same city, had taken the Medicine prize the previous year as an emigrant working in Cambridge. Leloir, who stayed, tells the room to have faith in the country's future. The 1986 printing was not retrieved here.
stops.quote: Senores, debemos tener fe en el porvenir de nuestro pais en un futuro mas o menos proximo...
stops.quote_source: Luis F. Leloir, 'Comentarios sobre la investigacion cientifica en la Argentina', conferencia de incorporacion, 19 June 1985, published 1986; quoted on Spanish Wikiquote, the 1986 printing not independently retrieved

segments.name: Recoleta, and the Name on the Door

stops.name: Buenos Aires, death after a day at the laboratory
stops.date_confidence: attested; both sources agree on the date and the cause
stops.campa: He comes home from the laboratory and dies of a heart attack the same evening, aged eighty-one. He had directed the institute for forty years and was directing it that day. Argentina declares national mourning. The two encyclopedic sources agree on the date and on the cause, which they do not agree on for much else in this life. The last working day is the detail the Argentine accounts keep: he was at the institute that afternoon and dead before the night was out.
suggested_refs: Argentine press coverage of Leloir's death and the declaration of national mourning, December 1987

stops.name: La Recoleta Cemetery, the family mausoleum
stops.date_confidence: the burial in the Leloir family mausoleum is attested; the exact day of interment is reconstructed as following the death by two days
stops.campa: He is laid in the Leloir family mausoleum at La Recoleta, among the marble avenues that hold generals, presidents and Eva Peron. No source gives the plot number. The cemetery stands a walk from the Facultad de Medicina where his Argentine training began fifty-five years earlier, and a longer walk from three separate buildings in which he worked out how a cell moves a sugar. The country buries its second science Nobel laureate in the ground it keeps for its first rank.
suggested_refs: The Leloir family mausoleum, Cementerio de la Recoleta, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Instituto Leloir, Parque Centenario: the renaming
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: In 2001 the Fundacion Instituto Campomar takes his name and becomes the Fundacion Instituto Leloir. It had already been given the Konex Platinum Prize in 1988 as the most important scientific institution in Argentine history to that date. It runs today with two dozen research groups and more than a hundred and seventy staff, on neurodegeneration, cancer, cell biology and plant biology, staffed since 1999 by open international competition. An asteroid, 2548 Leloir, carries the name as well.
suggested_refs: Fundacion Instituto Leloir, Avenida Patricias Argentinas 435, Buenos Aires; and minor planet 2548 Leloir
